And in some places, these rains unleashed catastrophic flooding & rockslides. * ELEVATION-ENHANCED WINDS. Higher elevations tend to get stronger winds in a hurricane, and this is an issue for Hawai'i, which has lots of residential neighborhoods thousands of feet above sea-level. These communities were hammered by damaging winds—even in locations far, far outside the hurricane's core. I've chased hurricanes in mountainous places before (Mexico, Taiwan, Jamaica, etc.), & this is some of the most stark elevation enhancement I've seen. For example, in beachside neighborhoods of Kona (where I'm staying), barely a twig or leaf was out of place after the storm, whereas neighborhoods in the nearby hills had wind damage. Hurricane-force gusts were measured in many places across the islands, with Mauna Kea summit (at over 13K ft) measuring a gust to a whopping 122 knots. * SNOW. Yep. On Mauna Kea Summit, it snowed. A total meteorological freak show. One last thing: There's a prevailing belief that the mountain peaks on the Big Island will always weaken approaching storms. LALA violated that belief. It did the exact opposite—strengthening into a hurricane as it neared the island.
